questions.q: What is the core trade-off between the shared and siloed tenancy models?
options: Shared is cheaper with weaker isolation; siloed has stronger isolation but more infrastructure to operate
There is no real trade-off — siloed is always strictly better
Shared tenancy always requires more infrastructure than siloed
Siloed tenancy cannot provide strong isolation
questions.explain: Shared pools tenants into one schema for cost and operational leverage; siloed trades that leverage for a hard isolation boundary.

questions.q: Why doesn't adding a tenant_id column to a shared table guarantee isolation on its own?
options: Because any single query that forgets to filter on tenant_id leaks another tenant's rows — the filter has to be structurally impossible to skip
tenant_id columns are not supported in most databases
Isolation is only a concern in the siloed model
A tenant_id column automatically encrypts each tenant's data
questions.explain: Real enforcement has to live somewhere a query can't bypass, like a security predicate on the table itself.

questions.q: What is the noisy-neighbor problem, as illustrated by Fabric Capacities?
options: One tenant's heavy load on shared compute degrades performance for every other tenant sharing that same capacity
Two tenants literally sharing office space
A problem that only affects siloed tenancy, never shared tenancy
A networking issue unrelated to compute or query load
questions.explain: A Fabric Capacity is a shared, metered pool of compute — one workspace's runaway query can throttle every other workspace on it.

questions.q: What kind of requirement forces the siloed tenancy model, according to this lesson?
options: A non-functional requirement like a compliance audit demanding provably isolated tenant data
A requirement to onboard new tenants as cheaply and quickly as possible
Any requirement at all, since siloed is always required
A requirement that only applies to small tenants
questions.explain: No amount of clever filtering satisfies an auditor who needs physical separation — that forces siloed, full stop.

questions.q: Why do most real multi-tenant platforms end up on the hybrid model rather than purely shared or purely siloed?
options: Because the right isolation level differs tenant by tenant — most tenants can be pooled, while large or regulated ones need siloing
Hybrid is required by law in every jurisdiction
Pure shared and pure siloed models are both technically impossible to build
Hybrid has no real cost difference from either pure model
questions.explain: The model should be decided against the actual requirement for each tenant, not applied as one house style across all of them.
